cards.q: What is the city block distance between two pixels, a and b, one at (308,154) and one at (293,193), in a 2D image (i.e., where D = 2)? Formula: d_cityblock(a,b) = Σ |a_k − b_k|, summed for k = 1 to D
method: Subtract the two row numbers and drop the sign. This is |Δi|.
Subtract the two column numbers and drop the sign. This is |Δj|.
Add |Δi| and |Δj|.
cards.check: City block is the largest of the three distances. It must be at least as big as the larger of |Δi| and |Δj|, and no bigger than twice that.
cards.trap: Adding the coordinates themselves, or adding a third number to the two differences. Write |Δi| and |Δj| on paper first, then add only those two numbers.

cards.q: What is the chessboard distance between two pixels, a and b, one at (44,148) and one at (196,96), in a 2D image (i.e., where D = 2)? Formula: d_chessboard(a,b) = max(|a_i − b_i|, |a_j − b_j|)
method: Find |Δi| and |Δj| as in Question 1.
Take the larger of the two. Do not add them.
cards.check: Chessboard is the smallest of the three distances. It equals one of the two differences exactly.
cards.trap: Adding the two differences. That gives the city block distance, 204 here.

cards.q: What is the Euclidean distance between two pixels, a and b, one at (105,141) and one at (119,85), in a 2D image (i.e., where D = 2)? Round your answer to 2 d.p. Formula: d_euclidean(a,b) = √((a_i − b_i)² + (a_j − b_j)²)
method: Find |Δi| and |Δj| as in Question 1.
Square each one and add the squares.
Take the square root. Round to 2 decimal places.
cards.check: The order is always chessboard ≤ Euclidean ≤ city block. Here 56 ≤ 57.72 ≤ 70.
cards.trap: Rounding early, or cutting the decimals off. Keep the full calculator value until the last step, then round.

cards.q: For the 8-bit greyscale image matrix shown below: Calculate brightness as arithmetic mean luminance. Round your answer to be 2 d.p. Formula: L̄_arith = (1 ÷ MN) × Σ L(i,j), summed over all pixels
method: Add all the pixel values.
Divide by the number of pixels, MN.
Round to 2 decimal places.
cards.check: The mean lies between the smallest and the largest pixel value. It is the largest of the three means.
cards.trap: Cutting the decimals off. 97.5556 rounds to 97.56, so 97.5 and 97.55 are both wrong. Always type two decimal places and round the second one.

cards.q: For the 8-bit greyscale image matrix shown below: Calculate brightness as harmonic mean luminance. Round your answer to 2 d.p. Formula: L̄_harm = MN ÷ Σ (1 ÷ L(i,j)), summed over all pixels
method: Work out 1 ÷ L for every pixel and add them all. Use the x⁻¹ key and keep the running total in the calculator.
Divide MN by that total.
Round to 2 decimal places.
cards.check: The harmonic mean is the smallest of the three means, and small pixel values pull it down. Here the arithmetic mean is 120.78 and the harmonic mean is 48.61.
cards.trap: Dividing the total by MN. That is upside down and gives a tiny number such as 0.02. MN goes on top.

cards.q: For the 8-bit greyscale image matrix shown below: Calculate brightness as geometric mean luminance. Round your answer to be ∈ ℕ. Formula: L̄_geom = (Π L(i,j))^(1 ÷ MN) = exp((1 ÷ MN) × Σ ln(L(i,j)))
method: Multiply all the pixel values together in one line on the calculator. The product is very large, so the display switches to × 10 to a power.
Leave the product on the display. Raise it to the power 1 ÷ MN, with the 1 ÷ MN in brackets.
Read the rounding line. ∈ ℕ means a whole number, so round to the nearest whole number.
cards.check: Add ln of every pixel, divide by MN and press eˣ. That route gives the same value. The order is always harmonic ≤ geometric ≤ arithmetic. Here 80.12 ≤ 97.85 ≤ 112.22.
cards.trap: Typing 97.85. The question asks for a whole number (∈ ℕ), so the answer is 98. Questions 4 and 5 ask for 2 decimal places and this question does not.

cards.q: For 8-bit greyscale image matrix shown below: Calculate contrast as statistical range. Formula: C_range(L) = L_max − L_min
method: Scan every row and mark the largest value, L_max.
Scan every row again and mark the smallest value, L_min.
Subtract. Range = L_max − L_min.
cards.check: Look through the matrix once more for anything larger than L_max or smaller than L_min. The range is a whole number from 0 to 255.
cards.trap: Missing the true smallest value. A one-digit value such as 4 is easy to pass over next to 10.

cards.q: For 8-bit (i.e, where bits-per-pixel b = 8) greyscale image matrix shown below: Calculate contrast as normalised range. Round your answer to 2 d.p. Formula: C_normRange(L) = (L_max − L_min) ÷ (2^b − 1)
method: Find L_max and L_min as in Question 7.
Divide the range by 2^b − 1. For 8-bit that is 255.
Round to 2 decimal places.
cards.trap: Picking the wrong smallest value. Here L_min is 2. Taking 16 gives 227 ÷ 255 = 0.89. The other mistake is dividing by 256.

cards.q: For 8-bit greyscale image matrix shown below: Calculate Michelson contrast. Round your answer to 2 d.p. Formula: C_mich(L) = (L_max − L_min) ÷ (L_max + L_min)
method: Find L_max and L_min as in Question 7.
Work out the top, L_max − L_min, and the bottom, L_max + L_min.
Divide top by bottom. Round to 2 decimal places.
cards.check: The answer lies between 0 and 1. It is close to 1 when L_min is small.
cards.trap: Dividing by 255. That is the normalised range in Question 8. Michelson divides by the sum L_max + L_min.

cards.q: For the 8-bit greyscale image matrix shown below: Calculate RMS contrast. Round your answer to 2 d.p. Formula: C_rms(L) = √((1 ÷ MN) × Σ (L − L̄)²), summed over all pixels
method: RMS contrast is the population standard deviation of the pixel values. Put the calculator in one-variable statistics mode.
Type every pixel value into the data list.
Open the statistics results and check that n = MN. A different n means a value is missing or typed twice.
Read σx. Round to 2 decimal places.
cards.check: By hand, √(Σ L² ÷ MN − L̄²) gives the same value. Here Σ L² = 172,089 and L̄ = 132.78, so √(19,121 − 17,629.94) = 38.61. The answer is also smaller than the range, which is 144 here.
cards.trap: Reading sx. sx divides by MN − 1 and gives 40.96 here. σx divides by MN, which is what the formula asks for. By hand, the usual slip is taking the root before dividing by MN, which gives √13,419.56 = 115.84.

cards.q: Given the 8-bit greyscale image matrix shown below and a scalar S = 5, enter the values of the output pixels at each coordinate following the operation: L + S
cards.varies: Nothing on Canvas. The test may still use other numbers.
method: Add S to every pixel.
Look for any result above 255. Write 255 there. This is called clamping to the upper limit.
If S is negative, look for any result below 0 and write 0 there.
cards.check: Every output value is between 0 and 255. Every value that was not clamped differs from the input by exactly S.
cards.trap: Writing 259 for 254 + 5. An 8-bit pixel cannot hold more than 255, so the answer in that cell is 255.

cards.q: Given the 8-bit greyscale image matrix shown below and a scalar S = 1.5, enter the values of the output pixels at each coordinate following the operation: L′ = S · L
cards.varies: Nothing on Canvas. The test may still use other numbers.
method: Multiply every pixel by S.
If a result is not a whole number, round it to the nearest whole number, with .5 going up.
Clamp any result above 255 to 255.
cards.check: S is more than 1, so every output is larger than its input. With S between 0 and 1 every output would be smaller.
cards.trap: Multiplying by 0.5, which gives 5, 10, 5 in row 1. That is only the extra half. S · L means the whole pixel times 1.5.

cards.q: Given the 8-bit greyscale image matrices shown below, enter the values of the output pixels at each coordinate following the operation: L₁ + L₂
cards.varies: Nothing on Canvas. The test may still use other numbers.
method: Add the two pixels that sit in the same place, one place at a time.
Clamp any result above 255 to 255.
cards.check: No output value is above 255. Look at the largest pair first, because the largest pair is the most likely to pass 255.
cards.trap: Typing 284 for 224 + 60. The sum is above 255, so the stored value is 255.

cards.q: Given the 8-bit greyscale image matrices shown below, enter the values of the output pixels at each coordinate following the image arithmetic operation: L₁ − L₂
cards.varies: Nothing on Canvas. The test may still use other numbers.
method: Subtract the L₂ pixel from the L₁ pixel in the same place.
Clamp any result below 0 to 0. This is an underflow.
cards.check: No output value is negative. A cell is 0 wherever the L₂ pixel is larger than the L₁ pixel.
cards.trap: Writing −50, −30 and −10. An 8-bit pixel cannot be negative, so those three cells are 0. Keep the order L₁ − L₂.

working: Row 1: 10 − 60 = −50 which is clamped to 0, 20 − 50 = −30 which is clamped to 0.

cards.q: Given the 8-bit greyscale image matrices shown below, enter the values of the output pixels at each coordinate following the operation: L₁ ∘ L₂
cards.varies: Nothing on Canvas. The test may still use other numbers.
method: The ∘ symbol is the Hadamard product. Multiply the two pixels that sit in the same place.
Here L₂ is a binary mask. Where L₂ is 1, copy the L₁ pixel. Where L₂ is 0, write 0.
cards.check: The output has a 0 in every place where the mask has a 0.
cards.trap: Doing normal matrix multiplication with rows times columns. The other mistake is copying the mask's 1 into the last cell. L₁ is 0 there, so the product is 0.
